reading.title: The Deep Sea Mystery
reading.text: More than 80% of the ocean remains unexplored, and its deepest parts, the abyssal plains, are among the least understood places on Earth. The pressure at such depths can exceed 1,000 times that at sea level, and sunlight cannot penetrate beyond 1,000 meters. Yet life thrives here in the form of bioluminescent fish, giant tube worms, and bacteria that feed on chemicals from hydrothermal vents. These vents, discovered in 1977, spew superheated water rich in minerals, creating unique ecosystems that do not rely on the sun at all. Scientists believe that studying deep-sea organisms may provide clues about the origins of life on Earth and even the possibility of life on other planets.

reading.title: The Invention of the Internet
reading.text: The internet began as a military project called ARPANET, funded by the U.S. Department of Defense in the 1960s. The goal was to create a communication network that could survive a nuclear attack by routing data through multiple paths. In 1969, the first message was sent between computers at UCLA and Stanford. By the 1980s, universities and research centers worldwide were connecting to the network. The invention of the World Wide Web by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 made the internet accessible to ordinary people. Today, over 5 billion people use the internet daily for communication, education, and entertainment.

reading.title: Why Leaves Change Color
reading.text: In autumn, the green chlorophyll in leaves breaks down, revealing yellow and orange pigments called carotenoids that were present all along. Red and purple colors come from anthocyanins, which are produced in the fall when sugars get trapped in the leaves. The intensity of autumn colors depends on weather: cold nights and sunny days produce the most vibrant displays. As leaves prepare to fall, a layer of cells forms at the base of the leaf stem, cutting off water and nutrients. Eventually, the leaf detaches and falls to the ground, where it decomposes and enriches the soil.
